name: Typecast — one-of-a-kind display font for your landing page, in 30 seconds
one_liner: Paste your landing page URL (or one line about your product) and Typecast generates a one-of-a-kind display typeface for your headline — drawn as code, not picked from a list — shows your real hero text in it, and gives you a TTF plus a copy-paste @font-face snippet.
problem: Every AI-built landing page looks the same: one audit of 120 AI-generated pages found 60% used Inter or no chosen font at all, and 61% kept default shadcn colours (buildtolaunch.substack.com). Indie builders shipping a site in an evening know their page looks generic but have no fast fix: commissioning a typeface costs thousands, Fontjoy only recombines existing Google Fonts, and handwriting tools like Calligraphr/FontMaker need you to fill in and scan a template. The one thing that instantly makes a page look like someone designed it — a distinctive headline face — is the one thing a solo builder can't produce in an evening.
target_customer: Indie hackers, vibe-coders and solo founders shipping landing pages (X build-in-public crowd, r/SideProject, Product Hunt launchers), plus designers who collect type. Free and open source; no buyer, the "payment" is the launch post and GitHub stars.
why_now: @nutlope showed on 30 Oct that a frontier-cheap model can draw usable original fonts: 36 fonts at $0.02 each with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on Together (https://x.com/nutlope/status/2116207994832838818). Together confirms that model only went serverless on 17-18 Oct 2026 at $0.30/M in, $1.20/M out (https://www.together.ai/models/deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017) — glyph-drawing as SVG paths at two cents a font is weeks old. opentype.js assembles those paths into a real downloadable TTF entirely client-side (https://github.com/opentypejs/opentype.js/). And the "AI slop design" complaint peaked this autumn, with nutlope's own anti-slop Hallmark skill at ~31k stars (https://github.com/Nutlope/hallmark).
comparables: Fontjoy (https://fontjoy.com/) pairs existing Google Fonts — no new letterforms. Mixfont and YoFont generate prompt-based fonts but are credit-gated (Mixfont: 50 free credits, 20 per font, 72 glyphs) and preview in their own specimen box, not your page. Calligraphr (€10/mo past 75 chars) and FontMaker (26 free chars) digitise your handwriting, a different job. font0 (https://github.com/Desmosy/font0) is the nearest open-source "prompt to font", but it only nudges the axes of a bundled variable font rather than drawing new glyphs. Font-swap extensions (Fontara, Tinkerfont, GetFont) restyle a live page but only with fonts that already exist. Nothing found does URL/description → original glyphs → your own hero rendered → free TTF.
market_note: Estimate, not measured: the audience is the hundreds of thousands of people shipping AI-built landing pages; willingness to pay as a product is low (Mixfont-style credits, maybe $5-10/font for an extended charset), but as a free open-source launch the return is attention and stars. A paid tier only makes sense at full charsets + multi-weight + commercial licence clarity, which is well past a weekend.
risks: The glyphs come out charming-but-broken and the output is embarrassing rather than postable. It is a one-time toy: you generate a font for your one site and never come back (partly fixed by the weekly Foundry shelf). Mixfont or YoFont ship the same "preview on your page" feature and are already commercial operations with an incentive to.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) The model actually draws legible, consistent letterforms — nutlope's 36 fonts suggest yes, but I have not seen the glyphs myself and consistency across 26 letters is the hard part; if it fails, fall back to 8-12 headline letters that spell the user's own word. 2) People care enough about a custom font to paste a URL — the AI-slop complaint is loud, but complaining is cheaper than adopting. 3) An unhinted, unkerned TTF looks good enough at hero size to be worth downloading (display-only framing makes this survivable).
first_customers: The build-in-public crowd on X who saw nutlope's font post; r/SideProject and Show HN; Product Hunt launchers rewriting their hero the night before; the Hallmark / anti-AI-slop skill audience (~31k stars) who already self-identify as hating default Inter.
validation_test: Before building the generator, post three screenshots of real indie landing-page heroes — one in Inter, two in model-drawn faces — and ask "which one looks like a company?" Pass: 100+ replies/quotes and at least 20 people asking where to get the font. Fail: polite likes and nobody asks. Costs one evening and about $0.10 of inference.
build_plan: Stack: Next.js on Vercel (one API route so the Together key stays server-side — Together has no browser-safe free tier), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 for glyph SVG paths, opentype.js in the browser to assemble and download the TTF, Jina Reader (r.jina.ai, free tier) to pull the headline and a one-line description from a pasted URL, html-to-image for the share card. Steps: (1) prompt the model for 40 glyphs (A-Z, 0-9, . , ! ?) as normalised SVG path strings on a 1000-unit em, three style directions per request, ~$0.06 a run; (2) render each candidate live in the browser with opentype.js + a Blob @font-face; (3) screen 1 = paste URL or type a line, screen 2 = your real headline in three new faces, pick one; (4) "Make it mine" → TTF download + @font-face snippet + an SFL-free licence note saying the glyphs are yours; (5) share card: your headline in your font, "made in 30s", OG image. Cut for v1: lowercase-only fallback if quality is poor, kerning, hinting, multi-weight, accents, any account or history, and screenshotting the real page (render just the hero text on a clean canvas — far more reliable than fighting X-Frame-Options).
launch_post:
Your landing page uses Inter. So does everyone's.

Paste your URL → Typecast draws a brand-new display typeface for your headline, shows your actual hero in it, and hands you the TTF. ~2 cents of DeepSeek per font.

Free, open source, no signup.
reasoning:
Typecast beat the others on three counts. It matches the taste file almost exactly — one input, one striking output in seconds, free, open source, and the output is the thing people share (roomGPT/Blinkshot shape) — and it rides a capability that is three weeks old, which is the LlamaCoder pattern the builder admires. It is genuinely new: I checked Fontjoy, Mixfont, YoFont, font0, Calligraphr, FontMaker and the font-swap extensions, and nothing does URL/description → original glyphs → your own headline → free TTF; the closest open-source attempt (font0) only tweaks axes on a bundled font. And the pain is expressed, not latent: people are loudly complaining that AI-built pages all use Inter, with a 31k-star skill built to fight it. The HackerTube bookmark was the loudest post of the night by a wide margin, but Canon (1 Nov) already mines exactly that dataset for exactly that audience, so every HN-video candidate was dropped as a repeat. No overlap with tonight's venture (Holdline, insurance certificates): different problem, different people, different bookmark. could_grow is true but weakly — a paid tier for full charsets and commercial licensing is plausible, though it would be a small design-tools business, not a venture.

Runner-up (Venture, 7.8): Three bookmarks pointed the same direction without naming the destination. Karpathy's HackerTube and the elvar Claude-skill thread both show the same 2026 capability shift — a long-context model doing in one pass what used to take a specialist weeks. Explee shows the commercial pattern: paste a messy artefact, get a decided action out. Serro shows the shape that actually sells — not a new agent, but the layer that catches the moment when fast work goes confidently in the wrong direction. Holdline is that layer applied to the least glamorous, most legally consequential hand-off in commercial insurance: an account manager issuing a certificate that says coverage exists when the endorsement forms do not say so.

Why it beat the others. Candidates 5 and 7 had the strongest investor tailwinds but the wrong shape for one builder working evenings — both are enterprise capital-goods sales. Candidates 2 and 6 died on the screen because well-funded or freshly-launched players already sell the exact workflow to the exact buyer. Candidate 10 and 11 were repeats. What survived was the step next to the hot category: everyone in 2026 is automating certificate *production* (COI ENGINE, Brokermatic, Certificate Hero, Caddi, QueryNow), and nobody at the small-agency price point is automating the *judgement* immediately before it. That is the classic boring-step-next-door wedge, and the deep research closed every obvious escape route for it except Certificate Hero extending its contract parser.

This builds on nothing in the library. The nearest neighbours are Rightsline (rights-vs-live-ad reconciliation) and Dockproof (retailer routing guide vs shipment) — Holdline shares their DNA of "a written requirement versus a system of record," but the buyer (independent insurance agency principal), the documents (subcontracts and ISO endorsement forms) and the wedge (an E&O-grade verdict log, not a chargeback or an ad pause) are all different. HoldLine from 2026-10-25 is an AI phone caller for B2B back offices and shares only a syllable; if the name collision matters, call it Certline.

The honest weak spot, and why this is 7.8 and not 8.5: the pain is loudly expressed by the people who do the work (the Reddit commercial-AM threads are unambiguous) and the legal consequence is documented in case law, but nobody publishes how often a requested endorsement is actually absent from the policy. So the ROI story today is hours and risk, not a measured error rate. Worse, Big "I" E&O guidance actively tells agencies to disclaim contract review — meaning the pain is expressed by the AM and partly suppressed by the principal who signs the cheque. That tension is the single thing to test this week, before a line of code: if principals say "we disclaim that," the same engine points at the insured contractor instead. Pass that call and this is an 8.5.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Holdline — contract-to-certificate gap checker for small commercial agencies. PICK. The only candidate where a named role with a budget line, a weekly recurring painful moment, a documented legal consequence and a gap that survived hard research all lined up.
2. Inbox-native COI drafter for small agencies — DROPPED AT SCREEN. COI ENGINE (founded 2026) and Brokermatic (founded 2026) ship exactly this, both explicitly inbox-first and AMS-free; Certificate Hero is funded and placed at Brown & Brown. Became Holdline's reshaped parent.
3. Carrier endorsement-request chaser (agent submits, tracks, verifies the returned form) — FINALIST, folded in. Real pain (carrier turnaround 1-3 days routine, 5-10 for complex; "submitted ≠ endorsed" is a documented trap) but too thin to be a company alone. It is now Holdline's step 4 and its recurring hook.
4. Subcontractor-side "can my policy meet this contract?" pre-signing report — FINALIST. Good latent pain and a real buyer (subs with many GC relationships), but research showed the holder side is crowded (Jones, TrustLayer, myCOI/illumend, Evident, Certificial, BCS at $3-30/vendor/yr) and sub-side willingness to pay is unproven. Kept as Holdline's documented pivot if the agency buyer disclaims contract review.
5. Long-lead electrical equipment PO expediting for data-center GCs (YC "Data Center Supply Chain") — DROPPED AT SCREEN. Enormous timing tailwind and multi-year transformer lead times, but 4castplus, Current SCM and SourceDay already sell post-award milestone expediting, the buyer is an EPC procurement org with a 6-12 month cycle, and it is far from this builder's skills and evenings-and-weekends reach.
6. Cross-tool outbound suppression and account-collision layer (from the Explee bookmark) — DROPPED AT SCREEN. Research confirmed the problem is real and the market fragmented, but the buyer is a RevOps lead at a company already drowning in GTM tools, the wedge requires write-blocking integrations into every sequencer, and it is a feature inside Clay/Outreach's roadmap.
7. Air-gapped open-weight LLM deployment-in-a-box for hospitals and defense suppliers (YC "AI for the Air-Gapped Economy") — DROPPED AT SCREEN. Clear investor pull and real budgets ($15k-$80k integrator deployments, $1.9-3.2M three-year clusters), but it is a hardware-plus-accreditation business with a 9-month sales cycle — wrong shape for a solo builder on evenings.
8. Permit correction-letter resubmittal from YC "AI for City Hall" — DROPPED AS NEAR-REPEAT. Backcheck (2026-10-28) already serves the permit coordinator with exactly this workflow; CivCheck/Clariti also now own the city side.
9. Jev-powered typed-decision router for insurance/claims triage (from the TypeSafe bookmark + YC "Vertical Foundation Models") — DROPPED AT SCREEN. Interesting capability at $0.042/M input tokens, but it is a primitive looking for a buyer; no named role complained about it. Its real lesson — cheap bounded decisions — is embedded in Holdline's met/not-met/cannot-confirm engine.
10. Creator-rights and Spark-code expiry tracker (from the TypeSafe UGC bookmark) — DROPPED AS REPEAT. Rightsline (2026-10-30) is the same buyer and the same core workflow.
11. HN-canon / HackerTube-derived consumer data toy (from the Karpathy bookmark) — DROPPED AT GENERATION. Canon (2026-11-01) already filed it, and it is a weekend build, not a venture.

PROJECT
1. Typecast — paste your URL, get an original display typeface for your headline + TTF. PICK: fresh capability (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 17 Oct), expressed pain, output built to be posted, no free equivalent found.
2. Foundry shelf of AI-generated fonts, browsable like a library — folded into Typecast as its return mechanic rather than run as its own project; a shelf with nothing to put on it is not a product.
3. HN Canon / HackerTube watch-history scorecard — DROPPED before research: direct repeat of Canon (1 Nov), same dataset, same audience.
4. HackerTube → YouTube playlist exporter by topic — dropped at screen: already requested and partly solved in the HN thread (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50319510), and hackertubes.com shipped a daily-mix clone within a day.
5. Teardown gallery: a public shelf of interactive machine simulators built with elvar's Claude skill — dropped at screen; it is a showcase of someone else's named project, close to the "don't clone a project in a post" line, and the builder would be curating other people's output.
6. "Slop score" — paste a URL, get graded on the 35 tells of AI-generated design — dropped at screen: awesomejev.com already ships exactly this with Jev, in ~250ms, and multiple anti-slop skills cover the same ground.
7. Startup follower-growth leaderboard from @benln's data, refreshed weekly — dropped at screen: X API access for follower history is the whole cost, xholic.ai and similar trackers exist, and the data is not the builder's to republish.
8. Micro-creator finder built on typesafe Jev at $0.002/creator — dropped at screen: it is the bookmarked project itself (shengkunye's launch), not an idea of ours.
9. "Who needs this?" — paste your URL, get a typed ICP card — dropped at screen: this is literally Explee from the bookmarks, and it drifts into the venture scout's lane (outbound/sales ops).
10. Caro-style "get it down to one sentence" tool for your own essay — dropped at screen: a writing tool, and Voiceprint (30 Oct) already serves writers checking what models do to their prose.
research_notes:
Venture: READING POT (3 of 3 used). Explee — confirmed it is an outbound agent at ~$0.04/email with $30 starter credits and a 105M-company database; useful as a pattern (messy input → decided action), not as a market. Serro — confirmed "agentic TPM," a context layer that catches agents building against stale assumptions; this framing directly shaped Holdline's thesis that the valuable layer is the one that catches a confident wrong answer. Jev/TypeSafe — confirmed typed decisions with probabilities at $0.042/M input tokens via Cloudflare, explicitly suited to bounded repeated decisions with escalation thresholds; this is the technical shape of Holdline's met / not-met / cannot-confirm engine and why "cannot confirm" is cheap to emit. I could not see any images; the elvar and benln bookmarks were judged on text alone and neither survived to generation.

SCREENING POT (6 of 6 used). (1) AI for City Hall / Plaid for Government Benefits — found CivCheck acquired by Clariti and Honolulu's 73→32.5 day review improvement; killed candidate 8 as a near-repeat of Backcheck. (2) Data-centre electrical supply chain — found 4castplus, Current SCM, SourceDay and dedicated expediting firms already covering post-award milestone tracking; killed candidate 5. (3) UGC rights/Spark codes — confirmed repeat of Rightsline; killed candidate 10. (4) Cold-outbound compliance and deliverability — confirmed Gmail's 0.1%/0.3% complaint thresholds and the 5,000/day bulk-sender rules, but the buyer was weak; killed candidate 6's first form. (5) Cross-tool suppression — confirmed a fragmented market with no authoritative pre-send layer, but concluded it is a feature inside Clay/Outreach; killed candidate 6. (6) Air-gapped LLM deployment — found NVIDIA AI Enterprise at $4,500/GPU/yr, integrator quotes of $15k-$80k, and a $1.9-3.2M three-year cluster estimate; real money, wrong builder; killed candidate 7.

DEEP RESEARCH POT (12 of 12 used) on the insurance-certificate cluster. Mapped the holder side (myCOI/illumend, Evident at $15-25/vendor/yr, TrustLayer free to 50 vendors, Jones, BCS at $0.95/vendor/mo self-service and $17.80/vendor/yr full-service with a $10,000 minimum, Certificial as the only carrier-sourced verifier) and established it is crowded and sells to the wrong buyer. Mapped the agency side (Certificate Hero $6.5M/RRE/Brown & Brown; COI ENGINE founded 2026, 1-10 staff, inbox-native; Brokermatic founded 2026, bulk renewals, ten founding agencies; Caddi $60k/yr + $5-15k implementation; QueryNow $2,500 sprint / $7,500 build / $1,200 mo; NowCerts from $99/mo; Qumis selling contract-requirements review to five of the 15 largest US brokers). Sized the buyer (Big "I" 2026: 37,000 agencies, 9.9 avg staff, 46% AI adoption up from 15%, contract review the #3 use at 35%, hiring the #1 challenge at 45%). Found the cost of the workaround (offshore insurance VAs $8-15/hr, licensed $15-30/hr; ReSource Pro and Patra on per-certificate production pricing; ~$3-6/task BPO reference). Found the pain in the users' own words (r/InsuranceAgent Feb 2026 commercial-COI-volume thread: one cert taking an hour across three stakeholders with AI, WOS and endorsements; 24 certs plus contract stipulations at renewal described as exhausting; a CL AM assigned 316 accounts/~400 policies). Found the legal teeth (West Bend v. Athens, Suffolk v. Illinois Union, Davis v. Erie denying AI coverage despite the certificate; T-Mobile v. Selective binding an insurer to an agent's certificate representation; Big "I"/IIAT E&O guidance telling agencies to disclaim contract review). Found the channel reality (Applied Vendor Certification and Vertafore Orange both approval-gated with no published vendor fees — so v1 skips the AMS). WHAT CHANGED: the deep pot is what moved the idea off certificate drafting, which was dead on arrival, and onto the uncovered verdict step; it also produced the price ladder and the stale-template renewal insight.

SHARPENING POT (5 of 5 used). Tested whether the reshaped idea holds: (a) confirmed no vendor sells standalone contract-requirement extraction to brokers — Jones embeds it in per-record holder-side pricing, Certificate Hero embeds it in certificate production; (b) confirmed Qumis does the work but sells to the largest brokers and risk managers on annual-plus-per-matter pricing, leaving the 9-person agency unserved; (c) confirmed AMS cert-holder records store holder details, not contract requirements, and that one published estimate implies ~56-83% of cert activity is renewal reissue — which is exactly where stale requirements propagate, validating the monthly re-check feature; (d) confirmed carrier endorsement turnaround of 1-3 days routine and 5-10 for complex, and that "submitted ≠ endorsed" is a real trap worth a tracking row; (e) confirmed the sales channel (clusters, Catalyit, Big "I" state associations, ITC Vegas) and a 1-3 month small-agency cycle at a $200-1,000/month approvable price. One thing the sharpening pot explicitly failed to find, and I am reporting it rather than papering over it: no source publishes how often a requested endorsement is actually missing from the policy. Pain stayed at 8 for that reason.

INVESTOR SIGNALS WEIGHED. YC W27 "The $15-an-Hour Expert" [latest] is the direct fit and is cited in why_now — Holdline is a credential-gated judgement (does this policy satisfy this contract?) handed to a non-specialist service rep. Also weighed: YC "AI for City Hall" (rejected, repeat of Backcheck), "Data Center Supply Chain" (rejected, wrong builder), "AI for the Air-Gapped Economy" (rejected, hardware sales motion), "Vertical Foundation Models" (informed the Jev-style typed-decision engine), a16z "Vertical AI evolves... to multiplayer" and "AI reinforces business models" (supporting, not load-bearing), and a16z "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (the underlying capability: subcontract PDFs plus scanned endorsement forms). No signal was adopted as the idea itself; each was used only to aim at a buyer my own research then confirmed.
Sharpening (7 to 7.8): ROUND 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6.0). The original candidate was "AI drafts the certificate from the inbox request." Research killed it: COI ENGINE (founded 2026, inbox-native, no AMS API, ~30-second draft), Brokermatic (founded 2026, bulk renewal cert packages), Certificate Hero ($6.5M raised, Brown & Brown, live ACORD editor), Caddi and QueryNow all do certificate production for agencies, and two of them launched this year with the exact "skip the AMS, work from the inbox" wedge. CHANGE: moved the product off certificate *production* entirely and onto the one step none of them close — the verdict on whether the policy's actual endorsement forms support what the holder's contract demands, plus the carrier endorsement request for each gap. EVIDENCE FOUND: COI ENGINE's own comparison page frames its differentiator as setup friction and speed, not coverage verification; Certificate Hero's contract parsing feeds certificate generation; a direct search for "who reads the contract and tells the agency which endorsements the policy lacks" returned no product doing it for small agencies — only Qumis, which sells to five of the 15 largest US brokers, risk managers, claims teams and law firms on annual-plus-per-matter pricing. Case law (West Bend v. Athens, Suffolk v. Illinois Union, Davis v. Erie, T-Mobile v. Selective) confirms the gap is consequential, not cosmetic. gap 6.0 → 7.5. Not higher: Certificate Hero already parses contracts and could extend; Qumis proves the capability exists upmarket.
ROUND 2 — weakest remaining: wedge (6.5) and market_pull (7.0). Worry was a long AMS-integration build and a buyer who might not have budget. CHANGE: dropped the AMS integration from v1 entirely (email-in, PDF-out), dropped ACORD generation, and pointed the sale at the agency principal/ops manager — who owns the E&O risk and the budget — rather than the AM who feels the hours. Added the monthly stale-requirement re-check so the product recurs rather than being used once. EVIDENCE FOUND: Applied's Vendor Certification and Vertafore's Orange Partner Program are both approval-gated with no published vendor fee schedule and no predictable timeline, so skipping them is the right call; COI ENGINE explicitly markets "no AMS API fees" as a feature, confirming agencies accept it. On budget: published comparables give a real price ladder a 10-person agency already pays into — NowCerts from $99/mo, AgencyZoom $149-349/mo, PINS ~$300/mo, QueryNow $1,200/mo plus a $7,500 build, Caddi $60,000/yr plus $5-15k implementation, and offshore insurance VAs at $8-15/hr with ReSource Pro selling per-certificate production pricing. Big "I" 2026: 46% of agencies now use AI (up from 15%), with contract review already the #3 use at 35%. wedge 6.5 → 7.5, market_pull 7.0 → 8.0. Not higher on wedge: verifying real carrier endorsement forms, including scanned proprietary blanket schedules, is genuinely hard and is the reason effort is 3+ months rather than weeks. Pain held at 8 — Reddit AM threads and the E&O case law are strong qualitative evidence, but no source publishes how often a requested endorsement is actually missing, so 9 is unearned. Timing held at 8.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the HackerTube data zip (6,454 videos, 150 topics, embeddings — confirmed it is rich but that Canon already owns it for us); DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on Together (confirmed real, serverless 17-18 Oct 2026, $0.30/$1.20 per M tokens, text+image in, outputs SVG path text not font binaries); and typesafe's Jev (real API, $0.042/M input, but the bookmark's project is the product). Screening pot (5/5): checked prior art for AI font generators, the HackerTube remix space (hackertubes.com already exists — killed candidate 4), the elvar teardown skill (real repo, elvarofficial/teardown), paste-your-URL ICP tools, and X follower-growth trackers. Deep research pot (8/8): confirmed opentype.js builds a TTF from SVG paths client-side; confirmed Together has no free tier and needs a server-side key (forces one API route); mapped the competitive set (Mixfont, YoFont, FontDance, Calligraphr, FontMaker, font0, Fontara/Tinkerfont/GetFont/flora) and found none combines original glyphs + your own page + free TTF; confirmed the AI-slop complaint is real and quantified (120-page audit: 60% Inter, 61% default shadcn colours); confirmed Google Fonts has ~556 variable families, which is what font0-style tools remix and why they are not the same product; confirmed iframe/CORS makes live-page restyling a trap, which shrank the build. Sharpening pot (4/4): checked weekly font-drop prior art (Fontshare, Font Bundles — curated, not user-generated), searched for existing slop-score and type-specimen-card tools, and checked client-side font tooling (harfbuzzjs/fonttools) — two of these four searches returned nothing usable, which is itself mild evidence the niche is open. Net effect: candidates 3-10 all died on research, the live-page-restyle ambition was cut, and the Foundry shelf was added and survived its check.
Sharpening (7.6 to 8.2): Round 1 — weakest criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: you make one font for one site and never return). Change: added The Foundry — every font anyone generates lands on a public shelf with the headline it was made for, and the site ships a weekly "ten new faces" drop you can browse and download. Research (Web Summary on weekly font drops) found Fontshare has "the weekly drop" and Font Bundles does a weekly free font, but both are hand-curated catalogues of professionally made fonts; no site publishes a continuously growing shelf of fonts generated by its own users, and the builder's taste file explicitly admires the "papers as a shelf of books" presentation. Usefulness 5 → 7 (a reason to return weekly, but I have no evidence people would actually come back, so not 8). Shareability 8 → 9: the shelf makes every generated font a public artefact with a URL and an OG preview, which is how these spread.
Round 2 — weakest remaining: buildability (7, unknowns around whether model-drawn glyphs assemble into a valid font). Change: dropped the ambition of re-rendering the user's live page (iframe/CORS trap) down to rendering just the hero line on a clean canvas, and capped v1 at 40 display glyphs. Research confirmed opentype.js builds and exports a TTF from SVG paths fully client-side with Path.fromSVG() (https://github.com/opentypejs/opentype.js/), and that Together needs a server-side key with no free tier, so a tiny API route is mandatory. That fixed the architecture but also confirmed real caveats (Y-axis flip, contour normalisation, no hinting/kerning) and that I have not seen the model's actual glyph output — buildability stays at 7, honestly. Score before sharpening 7.6, after 8.2.
prototype_summary: Typecast is a clickable prototype where pasting a landing-page URL generates three brand-new SVG-drawn display typefaces for your headline, which you can preview, download, embed and share.
